title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Connect the towing system to the ball mount's structural function.
student: Based on the photograph and component list, explain the primary structural function of the trailer hitch connection and the role of the ball mount.
instructor: The connection transfers forces between the trailer and towing vehicle. The ball mount carries loads applied through the hitch ball and transfers them into the vehicle-side receiver.

title: External Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the principal external loads and their application point.
student: Identify the major external loads acting on the hitch connection during towing and braking. Where are they transferred into the ball mount?
instructor: A horizontal towing/braking force and a vertical tongue load are transferred through the trailer coupler and hitch ball into the ball mount.

title: Support and Boundary Condition
learningObjectives: Identify the vehicle-side restraint represented in the model.
student: Identify where the ball mount is restrained by the towing vehicle. What motions and rotation are prevented in the simplified structural model?
instructor: The vehicle receiver provides the support. The receiver-side critical section is idealized as fixed, preventing horizontal translation, vertical translation, and rotation at that section.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace load transfer and anticipate internal resultants.
student: Trace the load path from the trailer structure to the vehicle structure. Identify where normal force, transverse shear, and bending moment are expected in the ball mount.
instructor: Trailer frame/tongue → coupler → hitch ball → ball mount → vehicle receiver. The equivalent receiver-side section carries normal force, transverse shear, and bending moment.

title: Critical Component and Section
learningObjectives: Identify the section selected for the strength check.
student: Which component and section are most likely to govern the simplified structural response? Explain why.
instructor: The ball mount is the component of interest, and the section near the receiver is selected as critical because it carries the combined internal forces and the largest load moment for this cantilever-type idealization.

title: Likely Governing Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Distinguish the locations of peak bending and transverse shear stress.
student: Rank the likely stress responses in the equivalent section and identify which one you expect to govern the first-yield check.
instructor: Combined axial and bending normal stress is expected to govern. Maximum bending normal stress occurs at an outer fiber, where transverse shear stress is zero for the idealized solid circular section. Maximum transverse shear occurs separately at the neutral axis and must not be combined with the maximum outer-fiber bending stress as though both occurred at one point.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the inputs controlling equivalent-section strength.
student: Identify the geometric, loading, and material properties that should influence the strength of the ball mount. Do not introduce point labels or instructor notation yet.
instructor: Relevant quantities include the horizontal and vertical load magnitudes, their horizontal and vertical offsets from the receiver-side section, the equivalent section diameter, the material yield strength, and the required factor of safety.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create an equivalent mechanics model from the real hitch assembly.
student: Convert the physical trailer-hitch connection into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model that preserves the dominant load path and geometry needed for the strength calculation. Show the idealized ball mount, vehicle-side support, applied loads, and key dimensions.
instructor: A suitable model is a planar equivalent member supported at receiver-side section C. Hitch-ball point A is horizontally offset by L and vertically offset by h from the receiver axis. Show horizontal load P, vertical load W, the critical section at C, and equivalent circular diameter d.
gradingNotes: Students should construct their own idealization before seeing the instructor reference image.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions defining the prescribed simplified model.
student: State and justify the assumptions used to reduce the real curved or forged ball mount to the assigned equivalent-section model.
instructor: Use a planar static model; replace the real curved/forged mount by the straight inclined load-path idealization; represent C by an equivalent solid circular section normal to the horizontal receiver axis; treat P as its normal force and W as its transverse shear; treat both loads as concentrated at A; assume a fixed restraint at C, homogeneous isotropic ductile steel, linear elasticity through first yield, and small deformation; neglect self-weight, local stress concentrations, detailed receiver/pin and ball/coupler contact, fatigue, dynamic impact, and exact forged geometry.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the equilibrium, stress, safety, and sizing sequence.
student: Before calculating numerical values, describe the sequence required to determine whether the equivalent ball-mount section satisfies the strength requirement.
instructor: Identify the support actions; use equilibrium to obtain reactions and internal N, V, and M at C; calculate A, I, and c; calculate axial and outer-fiber bending normal stresses; superimpose the governing normal stresses; calculate transverse shear separately at its own maximum location; compare the governing stress with Sy/nreq; and solve for a revised equivalent diameter if necessary.

title: Boundary Condition and Support Actions
learningObjectives: Interpret the boundary condition in the instructor reference model.
student: Using the instructor reference model, identify the boundary condition at C and state the three possible planar support reactions.
instructor: C is modeled as fixed. Its possible reactions are horizontal force Cx, vertical force Cy, and reaction moment MC.

title: Support Reactions
learningObjectives: Use planar equilibrium to determine the receiver reactions.
student: Draw the free-body diagram and determine the support-reaction magnitudes in terms of P, W, L, and h. Then substitute the assigned values.
instructor: The support forces oppose the applied loads: |Cx| = P = {{hitch_P_kN}} kN and |Cy| = W = {{hitch_W_kN}} kN. Moment equilibrium gives |MC| = Ph + WL = {{hitch_M_kNm}} kN·m.

title: Internal Resultants at C
learningObjectives: Determine the internal resultants at the equivalent receiver section.
student: Cut the idealized member immediately adjacent to C and determine the magnitudes of internal normal force N, transverse shear V, and bending moment M.
instructor: Because the equivalent section is normal to the horizontal receiver axis, |N| = P = {{hitch_P_kN}} kN and |V| = W = {{hitch_W_kN}} kN. Both offset loads contribute with the same moment sense, so |M| = Ph + WL = {{hitch_M_kNm}} kN·m.
commonMistakes: Do not resolve P and W along the drawn inclined load-path line; the assigned critical section is the receiver-oriented equivalent section defined in the model assumptions.

title: Section Properties and Stress Components
learningObjectives: Calculate circular-section properties and stress components at their proper locations.
student: For the equivalent solid circular section, determine A, I, and c. Calculate the uniform axial normal stress, maximum outer-fiber bending normal stress, and maximum transverse shear stress. State where each maximum occurs.
instructor: A = πd2/4 = {{hitch_area_mm2}} mm2, I = πd4/64 = {{hitch_I_mm4}} mm4, and c = d/2 = {{hitch_c_mm}} mm. The axial stress is N/A = {{hitch_sigma_axial_MPa}} MPa. The maximum bending stress at an outer fiber is Mc/I = {{hitch_sigma_bending_MPa}} MPa. For a solid circular section, the maximum transverse shear stress is 4V/(3A) = {{hitch_tau_max_MPa}} MPa at the neutral axis; transverse shear is zero at the outer fiber.

title: First-Yield Strength Check
learningObjectives: Evaluate first yield at the governing outer fiber without combining noncoincident maxima.
student: Combine the axial and bending normal stresses at the most highly stressed outer fiber. Determine the allowable normal stress and actual factor of safety, and decide whether the assigned section meets the requirement. Explain why the separate maximum transverse shear stress is not combined at that point.
instructor: At the governing outer fiber, σmax = N/A + Mc/I = {{hitch_sigma_max_MPa}} MPa. The allowable normal stress is Sy/nreq = {{hitch_sigma_allow_MPa}} MPa, and FS = Sy/σmax = {{hitch_fos_actual}}. {{hitch_strength_assessment}} The maximum transverse shear stress occurs at the neutral axis, whereas maximum bending normal stress occurs at the outer fiber where transverse shear is zero, so those maxima are not a same-point stress state.

title: Minimum Equivalent Diameter
learningObjectives: Size the equivalent circular section for the required first-yield factor of safety.
student: Keeping P, W, L, h, Sy, and nreq unchanged, determine the minimum equivalent diameter for which the governing outer-fiber normal stress does not exceed the allowable value. Round the practical recommendation upward to the nearest millimeter.
instructor: Solve 4P/(πd2) + 32M/(πd3) = Sy/nreq. The positive solution is dmin = {{hitch_d_min_mm}} mm; rounding upward gives {{hitch_d_recommended_mm}} mm. {{hitch_diameter_assessment}}

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
student: State the governing load case, critical location, governing mechanical response, factor of safety for the assigned section, and one mechanics-based modification. Identify at least one important limitation of the model.
instructor: {{hitch_engineering_assessment}} The receiver-side equivalent section governs, and combined axial-plus-bending normal stress controls the simplified first-yield check. A complete design must address local stress concentrations, actual receiver and pin behavior, hitch-ball/coupler contact, fatigue, dynamic impact, exact forged geometry, material/process details, and applicable towing requirements.
gradingNotes: Do not award full credit for an unqualified claim that the actual hitch assembly is certified or safe.
